title: USS Abraham Lincoln Passes 240 Days at Sea Without Port Call During Iran Deployment
excerpt: The Nimitz-class carrier has shattered the modern US Navy record for consecutive days at sea, raising concerns about crew welfare as food shortage reports and extended combat operations test the limits of naval logistics.
body:
• USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea for approximately 244 consecutive days without a port call, shattering the previous modern US Navy record of 206 days
  • Reports of food shortages and poor meal quality aboard the carrier drew national attention in April, though Navy leadership firmly denied the claims
  • The carrier's 5,000-plus crew has not had a port call since a brief stop in Guam on December 11-12, 2025 — normal deployments include port visits every 30-45 days
  • The extended deployment supports Operation Epic Fury against Iran, with more than 50,000 US military personnel in the Middle East

The USS Abraham Lincoln has now spent approximately 244 consecutive days at sea without a single port call, obliterating the modern US Navy record and raising mounting questions about crew welfare as America's sole supercarrier near Iran continues combat operations with no end in sight.

The Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, carrying more than 5,000 sailors and Marines, departed Naval Base San Diego on November 21, 2025, for what was originally a routine Indo-Pacific deployment. After a brief two-day stop in Guam on December 11-12, the ship was redirected to the Middle East and has not made another port call since — a stretch now approaching nine months at sea.

A Record Nobody Wanted

The Lincoln officially broke the previous record of 206 consecutive days at sea — set by USS Dwight D. Eisenhower during COVID-19 protocols — on July 6, according to Stars and Stripes. Lt. Cmdr. Alexis Travis, who serves aboard the Lincoln, marked the milestone on Instagram: "We've officially claimed the title for most consecutive days at sea for any modern aircraft carrier."

https://x.com/TheCradleMedia/status/2087097895501566409

Under normal conditions, a carrier makes port calls every 30 to 45 days to give crews rest, recreation, and time to resupply. The Lincoln has gone without one for over eight times that interval.

The Food Controversy

In April, a USA Today investigation reported that sailors and Marines aboard the Lincoln and the amphibious assault ship USS Tripoli were receiving poor-quality, small-portion meals. Families shared photos of sparse trays — boiled carrots, dry meat patties, and gray slabs of processed meat — and described crews going hungry.

"The food is tasteless and there's not nearly enough and they're hungry all the time. That kind of breaks your heart."

— Karen Erskine-Valentine, West Virginia pastor supporting Navy families

A former Marine whose daughter serves on the Tripoli told USA Today the crew was rationing food, hygiene products were running low, and there was no fresh produce. The suspension of US Postal Service mail to dozens of military ZIP codes in the region meant families could not send care packages.

Navy leadership pushed back forcefully. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle told reporters at Sea-Air-Space 2026 that the reports "grossly mischaracterized" food service and that some photos in the article were actually from a shore galley, not a ship. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth called the reports "fake news," posting on X that both ships had "30+ days of Class I supplies on board."

The Weight of Extended Deployment

The Lincoln arrived in the CENTCOM area of operations in late January 2026, joining what became Operation Epic Fury — the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran that launched February 28. Since then, the carrier has continuously conducted strike missions, with a sailor injured during flight operations on March 25 and nearly 300 US troops wounded across the broader conflict. Thirteen service members have been killed in action.

The ship operates alongside more than 20 US Navy vessels in the region, including the carrier USS George H.W. Bush, with over 50,000 American military personnel deployed across the Middle East. Iran has repeatedly claimed to have damaged or sunk the Lincoln — claims contradicted by satellite imagery showing the carrier operating in the Gulf of Oman.

Crew Welfare in Focus

Military families and veterans' advocates have raised concerns that the deployment's extraordinary length, combined with active combat operations and limited resupply, could take a toll on the crew's physical and mental health. The Navy has historically grappled with elevated suicide rates during extended deployments, and the Lincoln's crew includes sailors on their first deployment.

The Lincoln's ordeal marks the second time a carrier has set unwanted records during the Middle East conflict. The USS Gerald R. Ford previously set the mark for the longest overall deployment before being forced to withdraw for repairs in Crete after a shipboard fire destroyed roughly 100 beds and displaced about 600 sailors.

No official timeline has been announced for the Lincoln's return. With tensions between the US and Iran showing few signs of abating, the carrier's crew may have many more record-breaking days ahead.
